frameworks.name: Human-in-Loop LTV:CAC Scaling Ladder
frameworks.definition: A four-rung target ratio framework (3:1, 6:1, 9:1, 12:1) that sets the required LTV-to-CAC minimum based on how many of three business stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) involve humans versus automated/scalable systems.

frameworks.name: Attraction-Conversion-Delivery Scalability Spectrum
frameworks.definition: A three-axis diagnostic that rates each of a business's three core stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) on a 0-to-1 scale of human involvement, where 0 = fully automated/scalable and 1 = fully human-dependent.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the 3:1 LTV-to-CAC ratio, widely promoted by major tech companies as a universal rule of thumb, applies only under conditions of near-zero operational drag across all three business stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) — conditions that describe roughly 5% of businesses, typically pure SaaS products where ads drive straight to a checkout page and software handles delivery.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: All three stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) are automated with no human in the loop
Applies primarily to SaaS / software products

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC ratio target by business model

anchors.region: estimated share of businesses this applies to

bounded_by: Does not apply when any of the three stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) involves a human

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that introducing one human into any of the three business stages (attraction, conversion, or delivery) requires doubling the LTV:CAC target from 3:1 to 6:1, because human-dependent steps create capacity lumpiness that demands a built-in cushion to absorb the performance drop when adding new personnel.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Exactly one of three business stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) involves a human operator
claims.mechanism: Adding a human creates capacity lumpiness: when one employee's calendar fills, a second must be hired; the new hire underperforms the original, dragging the ratio below the minimum threshold unless the target was set 2x higher to begin with.

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC target by number of human-dependent stages

claims.text: Alex Hormozi sets a 9:1 LTV:CAC minimum for businesses where two of the three core stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) are human-dependent — the model he characterizes as typical for service business owners — because dual human stages compound the lumpiness and ramp inefficiency that must be absorbed during scaling.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Two of three business stages involve humans (e.g., human sales and human delivery)
Applies to service businesses as described in the transcript
claims.mechanism: Two human stages create two independent sources of performance variance: a new salesperson and a new technician both underperform incumbents simultaneously during ramp, requiring a larger ratio cushion.

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC target by number of human-dependent stages

claims.text: Alex Hormozi sets a 12:1 LTV:CAC minimum when all three business stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) are human-dependent, describing this as the minimum required to scale a fully labor-intensive business, not as a ceiling to aspire to.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: All three stages — attraction (e.g., manual outreach), conversion (e.g., phone or in-person sales), and delivery (e.g., service fulfillment) — involve humans
claims.mechanism: Three independent human stages create compounding variance across attraction volume, close rate, and delivery quality; a 12:1 cushion is required to remain viable after simultaneous ramp periods across all three.

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC target by number of human-dependent stages

bounded_by: A business can profitably operate at 6:1 and generate $1-2M/year without needing to reach 12:1; the 12:1 target is specifically for businesses planning large-scale growth

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that LTV:CAC ratios at or above 30:1 are both achievable and represent the signature of transformational business opportunities, citing four personal instances across his career where LTV:CAC exceeded 30:1 and the largest economic gains of his life occurred.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Distinct market opportunity windows with large arbitrage between CAC and LTV
Not a steady-state expectation — described as occurring during specific exploitable windows
claims.mechanism: Large LTV:CAC ratios emerge during windows of market arbitrage where customer value is high relative to the current cost of acquisition; these windows are finite and require iterating the money model until the lever cracks open.

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC ratio across business opportunity windows

anchors.region: minimum for large-scale growth (3 human stages)

bounded_by: Described as occurring during distinct windows, not as a baseline achievable by any business

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that there are only two long-term winning strategies for achieving extraordinary LTV:CAC ratios: driving CAC toward zero (via massive brand or viral product) or driving LTV toward infinity (via high-value enterprise contracts), and that at scale one of these two variables must approach an extreme — middle-ground strategies do not produce dominant businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to businesses aiming for very large scale
Does not mean mid-size profitable businesses cannot exist — those can operate at 6:1
claims.mechanism: LTV:CAC is a ratio; extraordinary ratios require at least one variable to approach an extreme. A middling CAC and middling LTV produces a ratio that is structurally capped, limiting the scale ceiling.
bounded_by: Companies can be profitable and sustainable at moderate LTV:CAC ratios (e.g., 6:1); the extreme-variable claim applies specifically to the largest-scale companies

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses Facebook as the canonical example of the near-zero-CAC strategy: by building a viral product that spread to billions of users at near-zero acquisition cost, Facebook generates meaningful revenue per user (estimated hundreds of dollars per year) on an enormous base, producing a massive aggregate LTV:CAC even without extraordinary per-user LTV.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Facebook does have some brand that offsets CAC; CAC approaching zero does not mean literally zero

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses Salesforce as the canonical example of the near-infinite-LTV strategy: Salesforce incurs large enterprise acquisition costs (bidding, contracts, sales cycles against competing CRMs) but offsets them with very high per-customer LTV — potentially $1-5M per enterprise account per year — achieving strong LTV:CAC despite high absolute CAC.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: Illustrative enterprise LTV range per Salesforce-class customer

bounded_by: Salesforce does have brand that offsets some CAC

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most business owners attempt to scale before their unit economics are validated — expanding headcount or opening locations while the model still requires iteration — and that this sequencing error is the primary cause of premature over-expansion, not a failure of ambition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founders tie ego to growth metrics (number of employees, locations) rather than to economic health metrics (LTV:CAC ratio, margin); this incentive mismatch produces premature scaling decisions.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that LTV in the LTV:CAC ratio should be measured as lifetime gross profit — not lifetime revenue — because gross profit is what is actually available to cover CAC and fund reinvestment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: lifetime gross profit or lifetime value
claims.mechanism: Using revenue instead of gross profit overstates LTV and understates the true ratio burden; only gross profit survives after COGS to be deployed against acquisition costs.

examples.text: In Gym Launch's first year, Alex Hormozi spent $100,000 acquiring gym clients while generating $10,000,000 in revenue — a 100:1 LTV:CAC ratio. Hormozi uses this as evidence that transformational arbitrage windows exist and that 12:1 should be treated as a minimum floor, not an ambitious ceiling. At the time, the business had automated attraction (ads), approximately half-human conversion support (some tech support reps), and a human-based phone sales team for closing.

Alex Hormozi illustrates human-driven lumpiness using a salesperson hiring scenario: a single high-performing salesperson has a finite calendar. Once it fills, a second salesperson must be hired. The new hire underperforms the original — possibly forever. If the business was running at a 3:1 LTV:CAC with one rep, adding the under-performing second rep drops it below 3:1. The 6:1 target provides the cushion to absorb this ramp period without going negative on the economics.

practices.text: Rate each of your three business stages (attraction, conversion, delivery) on a 0-to-1 scale of human involvement. Use the total count of human-dependent stages to determine the appropriate LTV:CAC target ratio (0 stages = 3:1, 1 stage = 6:1, 2 stages = 9:1, 3 stages = 12:1) before scaling.
Continuously iterate on the business money model — the combination of pricing, CAC, LTV, and margin — until a meaningful arbitrage window opens, rather than accepting current ratios as fixed.

Before expanding headcount or opening additional locations, verify that the current LTV:CAC ratio meets the minimum threshold for the business's human-involvement profile; scale only after the model is validated.
